title: Peripheral IV Catheter Insertion
summary: Inserting a short peripheral IV catheter into a peripheral vein for medication/fluid administration.
steps: Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Identify appropriate vein — antecubital, forearm, or dorsal hand. Avoid areas of bruising, infection, or AV fistula side.
Apply tourniquet 4–6 inches above the insertion site.
Clean the site with chlorhexidine or alcohol swab using a circular or back-and-forth motion. Allow to fully dry.
Remove catheter needle cap. Bevel up, insert at 10–30° angle in the direction of blood flow.
Watch for flashback (blood in the catheter chamber). Once visible, lower the angle and advance 1–2mm further.
Slide the catheter off the needle while stabilizing the needle — do not reinsert needle once removed.
Release the tourniquet. Apply pressure proximal to the site with one finger while removing the needle.
Dispose of needle immediately in sharps container.
Attach extension set or cap. Flush with 10mL NS using a push-pause technique to confirm patency.
Apply transparent dressing (Tegaderm) and secure with tape. Label with date, time, gauge, and your initials.
Document site appearance, gauge, attempts, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Avoid the dominant arm, areas of edema, or the arm with a mastectomy.
If two attempts fail, have another nurse attempt or consider escalating.
Assess insertion site every shift for signs of infiltration, phlebitis, or infection.
Replace peripheral IVs per facility policy (typically every 72–96 hours).
Use smallest gauge appropriate for treatment — 18g for blood, 20–22g for general meds.

title: Wound Care & Dressing Change
summary: Assessing and redressing a wound to promote healing and prevent infection.
steps: Review orders for specific wound care instructions. Perform hand hygiene.
Gather all supplies and set up sterile field if required.
Don clean gloves. Gently remove old dressing, noting type, amount, color, and odor of drainage.
Dispose of soiled dressing in biohazard bag. Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Don sterile gloves. Assess the wound — note size (length × width × depth), wound bed color, surrounding skin, and signs of infection.
Irrigate the wound with normal saline or prescribed cleanser. Use a 35mL syringe with 18g angiocath for 8psi irrigation if appropriate.
Pat the periwound skin dry with sterile gauze.
Apply appropriate dressing per wound type and provider order.
Secure dressing with tape or other appropriate method.
Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Document wound assessment including size, color, drainage, odor, periwound skin, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Obtain a wound culture before cleaning if infection is suspected.
Use Sterile technique for surgical wounds and clean technique for chronic wounds (per facility policy).
Stage pressure injuries (I–IV) and document accurately.
Refer to wound care specialist for non-healing wounds or wounds requiring debridement.
Assess patient pain before, during, and after the procedure.

title: Foley (Indwelling Urinary) Catheter Insertion
summary: Inserting a sterile indwelling urinary catheter to drain the bladder.
equipment: Sterile Foley catheter kit (includes catheter, drape, betadine, lubricant, syringe, collection bag)
steps: Verify provider order. Explain procedure to patient and provide privacy.
Position patient: female — dorsal recumbent (frog-leg); male — supine.
Perform hand hygiene. Open catheter kit using sterile technique.
Don sterile gloves. Organize sterile field — open all supplies onto field.
Place sterile drape under the patient's buttocks and fenestrated drape over the perineum.
Female: Separate labia with non-dominant hand (this hand is now contaminated). Use dominant hand to cleanse urethral meatus with betadine swabs — front to back, center, then each side.
Male: Hold penis with non-dominant hand perpendicular to body. Retract foreskin if present. Cleanse meatus in circular motion from center outward.
Lubricate catheter tip. Insert catheter gently into urethra — female: 2–3 inches; male: 6–9 inches — until urine flows.
Advance 1–2 more inches after urine appears. Inflate balloon with sterile water per catheter size (typically 10mL).
Gently pull back until resistance is felt — confirms balloon is in bladder.
Secure catheter to inner thigh. Connect drainage bag and position below bladder level.
Document insertion, initial urine output, color, clarity, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Use CAUTIs bundle: insert only when medically necessary, use aseptic technique, reassess need daily.
Never force the catheter — if resistance is met, stop and notify provider.
Replace foreskin to original position after insertion (prevent paraphimosis).
Assess for CAUTI symptoms: fever, cloudy/foul urine, suprapubic pain.
Remove catheter as soon as no longer clinically indicated to reduce infection risk.

title: Nasogastric (NG) Tube Insertion
summary: Inserting a nasogastric tube for feeding, medication administration, or gastric decompression.
equipment: Cup of water with straw (if patient can swallow)
steps: Verify order and assess for contraindications (facial trauma, esophageal varices, recent surgery).
Elevate HOB to 45–90°. Assess nares — choose the more patent side.
Measure tube length: earlobe → tip of nose → xiphoid process. Mark or note the measurement.
Lubricate the first 3–4 inches of the tube with water-soluble lubricant.
Don gloves. Insert tube through nare and advance posteriorly — aim toward ear, not top of head.
Advance tube while asking patient to swallow (or tilt chin to chest). If gagging is excessive, pause and allow to pass.
Monitor for respiratory distress, cyanosis, or inability to speak — if these occur, remove immediately.
Advance to the marked measurement. Secure tube temporarily.
Verify placement by: (1) aspirating gastric contents and checking pH ≤ 5.5 or using CO2 detector, (2) X-ray confirmation before first feeding.
Do NOT rely solely on air insufflation (whoosh test) — not reliable.
Secure tube to nose with tape or commercial holder. Mark tube at nare exit point.
Document insertion, tube length at nare, confirmation method, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: X-ray is the gold standard for confirmation before initiating feeds.
Recheck tube placement before each feeding and medication administration.
Assess nare for pressure injury — rotate side if long-term use.
Never insert in patients with basilar skull fracture — use OG tube instead.
Monitor for tube migration, especially after coughing or vomiting episodes.

title: Venipuncture / Blood Draw
summary: Collecting a venous blood sample for laboratory analysis.
steps: Review lab orders. Verify patient ID using two identifiers. Explain procedure.
Select site — antecubital fossa preferred. Avoid hematoma sites, edematous areas, mastectomy side.
Apply tourniquet 3–4 inches above site. Palpate and identify vein.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Clean site with alcohol swab using circular motion. Allow to dry fully (30 seconds).
Anchor vein with non-dominant thumb pulling skin taut below the site.
Insert needle bevel up at 15–30° angle into the vein.
Advance needle slightly after flashback. Attach first collection tube — blood will flow automatically.
Keep needle stable while changing tubes using correct draw order (see below).
Release tourniquet before removing needle (or as last tube fills).
Remove needle swiftly, apply gauze with firm pressure for 2–3 minutes.
Invert tubes gently per manufacturer instructions. Label at bedside.
Apply bandage. Document.
nursing_considerations: Draw order: Blood cultures → Light blue (citrate) → Red/Gold → Green → Purple/Lavender → Grey.
Mix tubes by gentle inversion immediately after collection.
If using a line draw, discard first 5–10mL per facility policy.
Do not draw from an arm with an active IV infusion in the same site if possible.
Apply pressure longer (5 min) for patients on anticoagulants.

title: Medication Administration (5 Rights)
summary: Safely administering medications using the 5 rights framework across all routes.
equipment: Administration supplies per route (oral cup, syringe, IV tubing, etc.)
steps: Right Patient: Verify using two identifiers (name + DOB or MRN) — ask patient to state their name.
Right Medication: Compare the medication label to the MAR — three times (pulling, preparing, administering).
Right Dose: Calculate and verify dose. Use a second nurse check for high-alert medications.
Right Route: Confirm the ordered route (PO, IV, IM, SQ, topical, etc.).
Right Time: Administer within 30 minutes before or after scheduled time (per facility policy).
Perform hand hygiene and prepare medication in a clean area.
Educate the patient on what the medication is and why it's being given.
Administer the medication per the correct route technique.
Stay with patient for PO medications until swallowed.
Document administration immediately in the MAR.
Monitor for therapeutic effects and adverse reactions per medication.
nursing_considerations: Also apply Right Reason and Right Documentation (7 Rights extended framework).
High-alert medications (insulin, heparin, opioids) require independent double-checks.
Never crush enteric-coated or extended-release medications.
Reassess patient's condition before administering — hold if contraindicated and notify provider.
Document any refused or held medications and clinical rationale.

title: Blood Glucose Monitoring (POC)
summary: Point-of-care capillary blood glucose testing using a glucometer.
steps: Verify orders or protocol (frequency, target glucose range, sliding scale).
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Turn on glucometer and insert test strip — confirm no error codes.
Have patient warm their hands or use the side of the fingertip for better blood flow.
Clean fingertip with alcohol swab. Allow to dry fully.
Lance the lateral aspect of the fingertip.
Apply gentle pressure to promote blood droplet. Wipe away first drop.
Touch second drop to test strip — do not smear.
Apply gauze to fingertip once sample collected.
Read result and compare to ordered parameters.
Administer insulin per sliding scale or notify provider if out of range.
Document result, time, and any interventions taken.
nursing_considerations: Rotate sites — lateral fingertips, avoid thumb and index finger.
Critical lows (<70) and highs (>400) require immediate intervention and provider notification.
Glucometer readings can be falsely low in severe hypoperfusion — confirm with venous glucose if concerned.
Change lancets each use — never reuse.
Document glucometer QC/calibration checks per facility policy.

title: Oxygen Therapy Administration
summary: Administering supplemental oxygen to maintain adequate oxygenation.
equipment: Oxygen delivery device (nasal cannula, simple mask, NRB, Venturi mask)
steps: Verify order including delivery device and flow rate, or titrate per protocol.
Assess baseline: SpO2, respiratory rate, effort, breath sounds, mental status.
Attach flow meter to wall O2 outlet. Attach humidifier if flow >4L/min.
Set prescribed flow rate.
Apply delivery device to patient:
Nasal cannula: prongs curve downward into nares, tubing over ears and under chin.
Simple mask: cover nose and mouth, mold nosepiece, secure straps.
NRB mask: pre-inflate reservoir bag before placing on patient.
Confirm SpO2 improvement. Reassess within 15–30 minutes.
Titrate per protocol to maintain SpO2 target (typically 94–98% or 88–92% for COPD patients).
Document device, flow rate, SpO2 before and after, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: COPD patients: target SpO2 88–92% — high-flow O2 may suppress hypoxic drive.
Provide humidification for flows >4L/min to prevent mucosal drying.
Assess skin integrity under mask/cannula — reposition and pad as needed.
O2 is a medication — always requires an order except in emergencies.
Monitor for CO2 retention in at-risk patients.

title: 12-Lead ECG Acquisition
summary: Obtaining a 12-lead electrocardiogram for cardiac rhythm and ischemia assessment.
steps: Verify order. Explain procedure to patient. Ensure privacy.
Position patient supine. Expose chest, wrists, and ankles.
Prep skin: shave hair if needed, wipe sites with alcohol, allow to dry.
Apply limb leads first: RA (right arm), LA (left arm), RL (right leg), LL (left leg).
Apply precordial leads in order:
V1: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border.
V2: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border.
V3: Between V2 and V4.
V4: 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
V5: Anterior axillary line, same horizontal as V4.
V6: Midaxillary line, same horizontal as V4–V5.
Ask patient to lie still, breathe normally, and not talk.
Acquire ECG tracing. Check for artifact or loose leads — repeat if needed.
Remove electrodes and clean gel from skin.
Document time of acquisition and deliver tracing to ordering provider promptly.
nursing_considerations: STEMI is a time-critical emergency — door-to-ECG goal is ≤10 minutes for chest pain patients.
Correct lead placement is critical — misplacement leads to false positives/negatives.
Baseline wander, movement, and loose electrodes cause artifact — reapply if needed.
Right-sided ECG (V3R–V6R) ordered when right ventricular MI suspected.
For female patients, place V3–V6 under the breast, not on top of it.

title: Central Line / PICC Dressing Change
summary: Performing a sterile dressing change on a central venous catheter or PICC line.
equipment: CVAD dressing change kit (includes sterile gloves, CHG disc/swab, transparent dressing, Steri-strips, mask)
steps: Review order and last dressing change date. Check for signs of infection or dislodgement.
Perform hand hygiene. Don clean gloves and mask. Apply mask to patient.
Carefully remove old dressing by stabilizing catheter hub — pull dressing parallel to skin toward insertion site.
Inspect site: redness, swelling, discharge, catheter migration (check external length vs. documented).
Remove clean gloves. Perform hand hygiene. Don sterile gloves.
Clean insertion site with CHG swab using a back-and-forth scrub motion for 30 seconds. Allow to dry 30 seconds.
Apply CHG disc (if used) around catheter at insertion site.
Apply transparent semipermeable dressing over site, starting at insertion point and pressing outward.
Secure catheter hub and tubing to prevent tension on the line.
Label dressing with date, time, and initials.
Document dressing change, site assessment, and external catheter length.
nursing_considerations: Change dressing every 7 days (transparent) or every 2 days (gauze) or when soiled/loosened.
Use CHG-based dressings when available — they significantly reduce CLABSI rates.
Never reinsert a migrated catheter — notify provider.
Assess for CLABSI signs: fever, rigors, erythema >2cm, purulent drainage.
Maintain strict sterile technique — central line infections are life-threatening.

title: Tracheostomy Care
summary: Cleaning and maintaining a tracheostomy stoma and inner cannula.
equipment: Tracheostomy care kit or: sterile NS, hydrogen peroxide (per policy), pipe cleaners/brushes, gauze, sterile gloves, spare tracheostomy tube (same size/type at bedside)
steps: Ensure suction and extra trach tube (same size and one size smaller) are at bedside before starting.
Perform hand hygiene. Don sterile gloves.
Suction the tracheostomy first if secretions are present.
Remove inner cannula if disposable — replace with new one. If reusable — place in hydrogen peroxide (per policy) and clean with brush, rinse with sterile NS, dry.
Clean the stoma site with sterile NS-moistened gauze, moving from inner to outer in a circular motion.
Replace stoma gauze dressing if soiled (split gauze around tube).
Change trach ties if soiled: have assistant hold trach tube in place while one set of ties is removed and replaced. Maintain one finger-width of slack.
Reinsert cleaned/new inner cannula and lock securely.
Assess stoma for granulation tissue, skin breakdown, infection.
Document procedure, secretion color/amount, and site appearance.
nursing_considerations: Never leave the tracheostomy unattended during tie change — accidental decannulation is a medical emergency.
Keep obturator and extra tube taped to head of bed at all times.
Perform care at minimum every 8 hours and whenever soiled.
Avoid over-suctioning — limit to 10 seconds per suction pass.
Inflate cuff appropriately if ventilated — check cuff pressure every 8–12 hours (goal 20–30 cmH2O).

title: Isolation Precautions (PPE Donning & Doffing)
summary: Proper sequence for applying and removing personal protective equipment (PPE).
steps: DONNING (putting on):
1. Perform hand hygiene.
2. Put on gown — tie at neck and waist.
3. Put on mask or respirator — ensure proper fit/seal for N95.
4. Put on eye protection.
5. Put on gloves — pull over gown cuffs.
DOFFING (removing — most contaminated items first):
1. Remove gloves: grasp outside of one glove, peel off. Hold in gloved hand. Slide finger under clean cuff of other glove, peel off over first glove. Discard.
2. Perform hand hygiene.
3. Remove gown: untie, pull from neck and shoulders, roll away from body, discard.
4. Perform hand hygiene.
5. Remove eye protection — handle by the arms/headband, not the front.
6. Remove mask — handle by straps only, do not touch front.
7. Perform hand hygiene immediately.
nursing_considerations: Contact: gloves + gown (MRSA, C. diff, VRE).
Droplet: gloves + gown + surgical mask + eye protection (influenza, COVID, RSV).
Airborne: gloves + gown + N95 + eye protection — negative pressure room required (TB, measles, varicella).
C. diff requires soap and water hand hygiene — alcohol gel is NOT effective against spores.
Perform hand hygiene at every step of doffing to prevent self-contamination.
